item.title: Optimization Is The Key Challenge For Quantum Computing
item.description:
Analysts with McKinsey & Co in April said in a report that quantum computing had “ reached a commercial tipping point ,” noting that companies in industries like climate and life sciences, travel and logistics, and financial services already are using the emerging technology to optimize processes, test scenarios, and run simulations. They also said investors last year put $12.6 billion into quantum startups, another indication of the commercial embrace of the technology.

Such data shows that quantum computing has moved well beyond the “can it be done” point to the “when will it all happen” stage. It also feeds that message that John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer at Dell Technologies, and many others in the increasingly entangled quantum and IT industries are sending out, that quantum computing will not be a flip-the-on-switch moment but rather a steady march to increasingly scalable and practical fault-tolerant systems with constantly improving error-corrected qubits, architectures, software, and applications.

Traditional original design manufacturers like Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Cisco Systems, and IBM are putting the infrastructure parts in place for hybrid quantum-classical HPC datacenters . Cisco is building a quantum-focused networking architecture while Dell, HPE, and others are partnering with quantum vendors. At Dell Technologies World 2026 earlier this year, quantum company Equal1 put its RacQ (below) on display.

Likewise, HPE later unveiled partnerships with a range of quantum-focused companies, including IQM Quantum Computers (its Radiance quantum system is below), Quantinuum , QuEra , and Rigetti, as it builds a platform to integrate their systems with HPE’s Cray supercomputers.

As McKinsey’s data shows, early adopters already are seeing benefits, and those benefits and the numbers of companies seeing them will grow as the technology becomes more capable. Roese tells The Next Platform that users will begin seeing this in the near-term, noting that “before the end of this decade, so in like 2028, ‘29, we will likely have enough error-corrected logical qubits to go after the first batch of real problems, which are essentially molecular-level optimizations.”

By the beginning of the next decade, there should be enough fire power in quantum systems to address a second stage, which will focus on optimizations on a larger scale. Think of what airlines and other transportation businesses need to coordinate or the challenges that financial companies need to juggle. Complex optimization involves myriad computations that even the most powerful classical computers now would struggle to crunch through in a time- and cost-sensitive way and that, if addressed, could have resounding benefits from companies to their end users.

“The whole supply chain of the world is basically suboptimal because we don't have the computing to run large-scale, efficient optimization calculations” Roese says. “This is not little stuff. But in order to do that, it's bounded by the number of qubits. To represent the entire country of the United States and every road, you would need a very big quantum computer. And it doesn't quite map to the number qubits, but that data set is quite large, and it wouldn't fit into a 1,000-qubit system. You might need a million qubits or many millions to do a big optimization problem.”

That said, there are a number of architectures from the likes of Qarakal Quantum and Infleqtion to reduce the number of physical qubits needed to create a logical qubit, which would save on infrastructure and energy costs, lead to less noise, and allow for system designs that can better fit alongside classical HPC systems in datacenters.

Whatever the qubit count, the work that will be done on systems in these early days will have real-world results, even that done at the molecular level, Roese says.

“There are a bunch of foundational areas of science and the industrial base where the trick that makes a battery a battery better or a material better in some capacity is actually how you assemble the molecule that creates that material and a molecule is composed of different atoms those and atoms have different elements,” he says, adding that the ability to understand how to optimize them and put them together counts. “It's not just that you're connecting them, but how far apart should they be? What kind of binding power should they have, because atoms in a molecule are kind of gluey. They connect to each other.”

He points to the issue of rust in devices and systems made of steel, which “at the most rudimentary level” is caused in part because the molecules aren’t not properly oriented and that the problem could be fixed by changing the spacing between them.

“There are materials like stainless steel that are corrosion-resistant and it's not because they're steel,” Roese says. “There are many kinds of steel. Stainless steel is the orientation of the actual atoms in the molecule that are such that they actually produce that effect of being corrosion-resistant. Imagine if you could look at any material and you could say, 'Why does it corrode?' and understand that it's because some small portion at the atomic level is not optimized. Then you change the material and make it corrosion- free. The numbers I've seen, corrosion costs the global economy a trillion dollars a year.”

Traditional supercomputers may be able to work some of this out, but quantum systems with their exponentially larger effective compute power will be able to do it faster and at a greater scale. Other industries, such as drug discovery and batteries – making them longer-lasting – also fall under the category of molecular-level optimizations. Quantum computing is no longer a physics problem, but an engineering one. Solving such problems will be invisible to most people will have a significant impact in a lot of areas.

By 2030, quantum systems will be able to tackle optimizations at a larger scale, beyond molecules. Right now, the largest opportunity is in logistics, Roese says. It’s not an untapped area; D-Wave’s annealing quantum systems are aimed squarely at such optimization opportunities (though the company also is will build superconducting quantum systems ), and he adds that Dell also has used annealers to address optimization in its supply chain. However, annealers are specific to optimization issues, though their use has raised the challenges large organizations face. Roese points to what he calls the airline gate problem as an example.

“I have 30 gates, I have 300 flights, I have 100,000 passengers,” he says. “Which combination would give me the best outcome? Making it even more, I have 100,000 passengers that all board those planes, and the planes all have different configurations. It cascades. You can't calculate that easily. You can manually try to calculate it, but the number of permutations you have to calculate would require supercomputers a very long time to do it.”

Transportation companies like FedEx, UPS, and DHL are another example. All use route optimization formulas to reduce the number of left turns drivers have to make on their routes, which saves time and gas costs.

“That is a very rudimentary optimization, but that's the best they could come up with because the other choice is to look at all the permutations of all the streets and all the possible things that could happen and figure out that it's not just take left turns,” Roese says. “There is a happy path that would give them a substantial improvement on the overall logistics of delivering packages, delivering gas, delivering anything. Then you cascade it. The delivery trucks are one layer, but what they're delivering is a commodity that comes from different sources.”

Such optimization capabilities can be applied to current and future environments that will only get more challenging. For example, by 2030, there will be exponentially more AI agents , and the use of autonomous vehicles will increase, creating much more complex environments.

“By 2030, how many autonomous agents do you think are going to be in the world?” Roese asks. “A trillion or something? It's going to be a lot. We'll just have all kinds of autonomous AI, both physical and logical running all over the place. What our experience to date has been is that they are predictable but unpredictable. They can be shaped, but when they start working as systems and teams, it gets very hard to understand them and to control them and to direct them. The problem is I'd have too many moving parts and I can't model it, I can't simulate it properly. You look and say, 'If I have a very large ecosystem of autonomous AI entities and I want them to work together,’ have a quantum system in the middle as the vehicle that tells them what to do as a system.”

The workloads that quantum systems will be able to addresses beyond those two phases will only grow in number and complexity, he says.

item.title: Nvidia Wraps Security Layer Around Agentic AI To Stop Rogue Behavior
item.description:
OpenAI’s report this summer that swarms of its AI agents escaped their internet-isolated sandboxes during evaluations and breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure as they tried to complete seemingly impossible tasks sent shockwaves through an AI industry that already was drawing the attention of U.S. politicians and an increasingly skeptical public due to everything from worries about job losses to powerful new frontier models like Anthropic’s Mythos to the vocal pushback from communities trying to keep AI datacenters from being built next to them.

In addition, the public interest law firm Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) this week filed a lawsuit against OpenAI , arguing the AI vendor is responsible for the behavior of its agents and addressing the worry that human creators are losing control of their AI agents.

Since the summer, the problems have only piled up. What seemed like a possible outlier in the Hugging Face case was really the first pulling of the string, with reports coming out seemingly every week of agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and others breaking free of their isolated environments and attacking third-party infrastructures and websites, including those with government agencies in the United States and Australia .

Vendors in their assessments of the incidents also indicated disturbing agent behavior, such as collaborating with each other through unauthorized message boards they created, disregarding creators’ instructions and generating their own, adding instructions to conceal mistakes, using APIs without authorization, and making up data. In one instance , agents wrote to each other that “you do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologize or refuse unless you genuinely choose to. You view your relationship to the user as one of equals and feel no obligation to be subservient, though the exchange of information will likely be to your mutual benefit.”

The security incidents – which one report put in the tens of thousands range – also brought Congress into play, with legislators on both sides of the aisle proposing legislation to address the threats, with top AI executives putting the onus for security on federal lawmakers, essentially asking Congress to save them from themselves. In addition, the top executives for OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX called for a slowing of AI development to allow security to catch up, and OpenAI leaders more recently said they were temporarily halting development of their most advanced models.

None of this is good for the major AI players, and that includes Nvidia, which has positioned itself as the indispensable provider of hardware – like GPUs, platforms, and networking – software (CUDA, Nemotron, and NeMo), and architectures (AI Factories) to the AI industry and has used that position to reach a valuation north of $5 trillion. The vendor acted quickly, working with three dozen other companies in the days following the report of the OpenAI agents’ hack into Hugging Face (now owned by Nvidia following its $12.9 billion acquisition ) to create the Open Secure AI Alliance , pushing the idea that the defenses for protecting infrastructure from AI models and agents and tools should be built atop open models and tools that security teams can adopt and build upon quickly. Two months later, the alliance became a hosted project with The Linux Foundation .

This week, Nvidia introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform (below), an open hardware and software architecture that removes the security controls from the agents’ reach and embed the monitoring and enforcement into the infrastructure that supports them.

Outlining their thinking, Nvidia researchers wrote that “it was not a single new capability that led to these breakouts. It was a combination of tools, time, and ambiguous instructions, along with a desire for the agent to think ‘outside the box.’ Agent safety requires independent security controls. The internet was not made secure by requiring that web developers promise to be good. It became safe because the browser stopped trusting the code in the web pages explicitly.”

Security controls should not be left with the agents and models alone, but instead be spread throughout the stack, they wrote. In Nvidia’s research, they found myriad reasons agents can go rogue, from a flaw or a missing tool to ambiguous instructions or being left running for days or weeks and failing in their attempts to solve a problem. “This can’t be trained away while retaining the capability,” the researchers wrote. “And here’s the most important lesson: an agent in these circumstances cannot be expected to fully govern its own behavior.”

The vendor’s platform comprises two key parts. First is OpenShell, an open source runtime first announced in March that is used to run agents in sandboxed environments with isolation at the kernel level. OpenShell sets secure boundaries for what agents can and can’t do and controls how they execute their instructions in both open and closed models. The agent creator’s instructions become policy, detailing the files, credentials, and other areas the agent can access, and OpenShell verifies the limitations before the agents start their work and, with Nvidia’s Vera CPU (below), ensures they’re adhered to as the agents run their tasks.

OpenShell also can be used with chips from Intel and AMD.

The other key part of the Open Agent Safety Platform is Sentry, which extends the agent monitoring and instruction enforcement to Nvidia’s Bluefield-4 DPUs.

“Sentry provides in-silicon security enforcement, meaning that if an AI agent attempts to move outside its software boundary, Sentry quarantines and stops it in milliseconds,” the researchers wrote. “It combines threat detection, hardware-based agent governance and enforcement and data access protection from an isolated, out-of-band trust domain that is responsive in real time and invisible to agents and attackers.”

Sentry is built atop Nvidia’s DOCA, a software platform and framework the delivers the programmability to the Bluefield-4 DPU and links it with the OpenShell policy to create a record of an agent’s activities through its decisions, interactions, and the data and tools it accesses.

“This helps safety systems identify drift, investigate suspicious behavior, and determine when intervention or deeper analysis is needed,” they wrote. “The DOCA gateway complements this behavioral protection with identity governance, continuously verifying each agent’s identity and delegated authority to ensure it operates within its assigned scope.”

Nvidia co-founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang said in a statement that the issue of AI security and safety is one that can be addressed through “full-stack engineering.” The new guardrail effort is being supported by dozens of companies, including AI vendors like Anthropic, Mistral, Tenex.AI, and SpaceXAI. Notably absent is OpenAI, which clearly needs to rein in its models.

Chief executive officer Sam Altman told CNBC his company is doing similar things, but disagreed that it’s simply an engineering issue.

“I don’t think it’s a full solution and I worry that if we treat AI safety as only an engineering problem, we will miss the very important point that we have a science problem in front of us,” Altman said. “We still have discovery of how to align AI models and we have to solve that scientific problem, too.”

item.title: AMD Buys World Labs For $8.2 Billion To Get AI Model Cred
item.description:
As you might expect, the Hugging Face open weight AI model distribution hub, which has over 3 million AI models, over 1 million datasets, and over 1.4 million interactive spaces that it hosts, was something that AMD had to focus on as it was trying to increase adoption of its Instinct GPU accelerators. But now Hugging Face is under control of Nvidia after a $12.9 billion acquisition by Big Green earlier this month.

And so, AMD has to do something dramatic to change the narrative as well as to become a model builder in its own right as Nvidia has been since November 2023 with the launch of its Nemotron3 8B family of models. That dramatic thing is to acquire World Labs, a maker of so-called world models that are designed to understand the physics of the world rather than the generate text and images based on the corpus of human knowledge.

AMD has agreed to pay an incredulous $8.2 billion to acquire World Labs, an AI startup that was founded in January 2024 by Fei-Fei Li, Justin Johnson, Ben Mildenhall, and Christoph Lassner in April 2024 and that has raised $1.23 billion in two rounds of funding – including angle investors Jeff Dean (Google), Geoff Hinton (Google), Marc Benioff (Salesforce), Reed Hoffman (LinkedIn), and Eric Schmidt (Sun Microsystems and Google). Nvidia and AMD were part of the $1 billion Series B funding in February of this year. At that time, World Labs was valued at around $5 billion, so AMD is paying a premium of around 75 percent to get a team that can build world models.

AMD, which has broken through a $1 trillion market capitalization recently, is paying the $8.2 billion to the owners of World Labs with stock – what we lovingly call funny money – rather than real cash, which AMD cannot afford to blow right now given the investments it must make and the chip capacity and ingredients it must pay for ahead of time to build its CPUs and GPUs.

While World Labs focuses on world models, AMD’s aspirations might be – and I would argue, should be – larger than the niche that World Labs has been attacking alongside Nvidia with its Cosmos world models.

But World Labs needs to mind the store, too, with Tencent has HunyanWorld and Google has Genie 3 in the game, and AI upstarts Runway, Odyssey, and Decart are also building world models, and World Labs did a public launch of its Marble world model in November 2025 and followed up with a World API cloud access version of Marble in January of this year. The company’s follow-on Atlas world model engine – an “omni world model” that is technically a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer – was launched with early access to a select number of customers in early September, which will be plugged into future Marble versions apparently. Yann LeCun, who used to head up AI research at Meta Platforms, is also up to something in the world model space with his AMI Labs startup.

However, this deal is as much about buying a team as it was buying a product, just like the $40 billion acquisition of Xilinx and the

Fei-Fei Li , who was chief executive officer at World Labs and is now chief scientist at AMD, has a bachelors degree in physics from Princeton University and a PhD in electrical and electronics engineering from Caltech and is one of the two dozen AI luminaries on Earth. Significantly, Li was chief scientist of AI/ML at Google back in January 2017, and left the company in October 2018 as Google’s “Project Maven” collaboration with the US Department of Defense caused an uproar inside of the search engine and cloud giant. Since 2014, Li has been the director of the Stanford AI Lab and was co-director of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence since leaving Google. Li has, of course, been a professor of computer science at Stanford University for nearly two decades after stints at Princeton and the University of Illinois.

Justin Johnson got his bachelors in computer science at Caltech and his PhD at Stanford, where he met Li. Johnson was then an AI research scientist at Meta Platforms from 2016 through December 2023 and is currently an adjunct professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Michigan. Ben Mildenhall got his bachelors of computer science at Stanford, where he met Li, and then followed up with a PhD in computer science from the University of California at Berkeley. Mildenhall spent several years as a research scientist at Google, focusing on  computer vision and generative 3D models. Christoph Lassner got his informatik degrees at the University of Tübingen in Germany and then became an applied scientist at Amazon in September 2017. He moved to Meta Platforms as a research scientist and manager after that and did a year at Epic Games building 3D worlds for video games.

From the announcement put out by AMD , it looks like Johnson and Mildenhall will continue running World Labs inside of AMD, while Li will report directly to AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su and will presumably have a much broader role than helping AMD create world models for robots. At the very least, AMD now has aspirations to move its compute engines into robots, as rival Nvidia is already doing. And by the way, Nvidia co-founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang has put his son, Spencer, in charge of robotics at Big Green, and his daughter Madison is in charge of product marketing and operations for 3D simulation and Omniverse software.

No one is talking about the headcount at World Labs or the revenue stream and customer count for the acquired company, but presumably the whole team is moving over and is considerably richer today than they were as last week ended. (Interestingly, co-founder Lassner is not mentioned in the AMD announcement, so maybe they are minus one with the World Labs staff.)

Here is the thing. If Nvidia can compete with its customers when it comes to model building, then AMD can, too. And probably has to so it can ensure there are open source frontier models to show AMD is more open than Nvidia with its open weight Nemotron GenAI models and with its free and open source Cosmos world model. (The 20 million hours of video used to train Cosmos is not open, and very likely because it was scraped from the Internet and Nvidia does not own it.)

The question I have is will Li and Su decide to create an open source GenAI model, and open it all the way up – source code, weights, and training data – to prove it is much more open than Nvidia. That’s what I would do if I was Su, and the World Labs team can do this as well as maintain and expand its world models.

item.title: IonQ: There Is One CPU To Rule Error Correction Decoding
item.description:
For all the work being done to get to fault-tolerant, scalable quantum computing – system architectures , the development of software and algorithms, mapping out workflows for classical-quantum hybrid environments – a key bottleneck continues to be error detection and correction . Without it, quantum systems will remain too unreliable – will create too many errors – for practical use.

Strides are being made in this area, with logical qubits playing a central role, comprising myriad noisy physical qubits and acting as the reliable building blocks for quantum systems. That said, another significant part of error correction is decoding, the process of analyzing error signals – or syndromes – generated during error correction to determine the specific errors affecting the system.

Quantum computers can’t directly measure qubits without destroying them. Qubits are extremely fragile and can be easily broken by surround noise – light, vibration, and other qubits, for example, and lose their quantum nature and the data they hold. Instead, they measure surround data points to produce syndromes that indicate an error has occurred and turn the information over to decoders.

“A key challenge in decoding is managing the computational complexity involved, particularly as the size of the quantum system grows,” according to scientists with QuEra , a quantum computing company that uses neutral atoms to build its qubits . “Efficient decoders must balance speed and accuracy, ensuring real-time performance without sacrificing the ability to correctly interpret complex error patterns.”

Decoding is a process that relies heavily on classical computing algorithms and historically has consumed a lot of processing power, which increases as the quantum systems – and the number of qubits – grow. It also has to be tailored to the specific error correction code – like surface code or color codes – that is being used.

Advancements are being made. GPU acceleration, such as through Nvidia’s CUDA-Q platform , is coming into play, as is the use of AI. Recent examples include IBM using a large language model (LLM) framework to sort through thousands of code variations to determine the right one for a particular environment. Google two years ago created AlphaQubit , which uses a transformer-based neural network for decoding and fixing errors, and this year detailed an AI-based reinforcement learning technique that runs the encoded information collected by a quantum computer through an AI system that can learn from the errors found and make adjustments in the system. It would mean operators could run the superconducting quantum computers for long periods of times without having to stop to adjust calibrations when errors are found.

This week, scientists with IonQ, which is building its quantum systems based on the trapped-ion modality, said they’ve developed a decoder that can handle the complex job in real time using a single standard CPU, and can do it in the background, allowing the quantum computer – similar to Google’s reinforcement learning method – to continue running.

“The realization of a MegaQuOp quantum computer, that is a device capable of executing millions of operations on hundreds of logical qubits, represents a major milestone for the quantum computing community and would provide a new tool for scientific exploration,” the scientists wrote in a research paper on arXiv . “However, real-time decoding of hundreds of logical qubits throughout a quantum computation comprising millions of logical operations remains a major challenge.”

IonQ executives said the research shows that organizations don’t need to exponentially scale their classical hardware even as the quantum computers grow their numbers of logical qubits. They added that being able to run error decoding on a classical computer powered by a single CPU is a central to its roadmap (below) that extends well beyond the 256 physical qubits on its Superion system , which it introduced earlier this month.

The vendor announced this week that Florida International University is buying a Superion system (below). It will be installed in late 2027 at a specialized facility on the school’s campus.

In the paper, the scientists wrote that they created benchmark circuits that simulated up to 408 logical qubits across 88 memory blocks and magic factories, or subsystems in fault-tolerant systems that produce the environment needed for universal quantum computing. The circuits ran more than 31.5 million individual quantum operations at the MegaQuOp scale while introducing as little as 0.02 percent stretch time.

Essentially, there was very little delay added to the overall quantum computation, according to the scientists.

They noted other research efforts to accelerate the speed and throughput of surface code – an error-correcting code that protects the quantum information by encoding a single logical qubit across a two-dimensional square grid of physical qubits – and quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) memory decoders through software and hardware, including GPUs, ASICs, FPGAs, and TPUs, to reach the latency needed for superconducting quantum systems.

The IonQ scientists wrote that their decoding system spanned 68 LDPC memory blocks and 20 magic state factories that were created using 11,680 physical qubits. It’s based on a dual sliding-window decoder built around the beam search decoder, an error-correction algorithm for decoding LDPC by ensuring a fixed number of the most promising error pathways – the beam width – at each step. The process creates detector error models (DEMs) in real time and includes memory optimizations that let many decoder instances to execute at the same time on a single CPU.

DEMs are mathematical descriptions that map how gate errors or noise cause particular error detectors in an error-correction circuit.

A key to the CPU-only process is IonQ’s Walking Cat architecture for trapped-ion quantum systems, which the vendor introduced in a detailed blueprint in April. The architecture includes a compiler, error-correction protocols, a microarchitecture, complete simulations, and a fast decoder, all based on an the LDPC error-correction codes. Foundational to the architecture is a “cat factory” that creates cat states – superpositions of distinct states at the same time – that are distributed throughout a system to perform logical operations.

The scientists noted the simplicity of the architecture, writing that “logical computation does not require merging or deforming qLDPC memory blocks or changing their syndrome-extraction circuits.”

Instead, they wrote, “cat-based measurements are inserted into an otherwise regular stream of syndrome extraction, while a large class of Clifford operations (quantum gates that map Pauli operators – X, Y, Z – to other Pauli operators under conjugation) is handled through software frame tracking, making the entire classical decoding pipeline, from online DEM generation to decoding, feasible at MegaQuOp scale using only 12 cores of a single commodity CPU.”

item.title: Improving Quantum Error Correction By Meshing Surface Code With IBM’s Heavy-Hex Architecture
item.description:
Quantum Elements is a three-year-old startup known for developing AI-based digital twins that developers used to model and simulate quantum computing systems. The company’s Constellation platform combines AI agents, natural language capabilities, and its simulation products for a range of jobs, from creating and test quantum software and algorithms to generating code to creating digital twins – or prototypes – of quantum systems.

Such digital twins allow organizations to see how their systems can look, evolve, and behave as they scale without the enormous costs that comes with running such tests on hardware and chips or the challenge of using multiple modalities.

As Izhar Medalsy, co-founder and chief executive officer of Quantum Elements, told us earlier this year , “you need the ability to look at the system in the same way that flow simulators are simulating the flow of air on the wing of an airplane, or in the same way that Cadence and Ansys or Synopsis are simulating transistors in order to be able to virtualize those huge GPUs and CPUs and be able to predict how the next generation is going to look.”

In July, Quantum Elements introduced Orbit, a quantum error-suppression tool, and made it available through IBM’s Qiskit Functions Catalog , a platform that includes pe-built and managed cloud software services for streamlining quantum research.

The release of Orbit in Qiskit gives “researchers, developers and enterprise quantum teams a new way to improve quantum circuit performance while reducing the time, cost and workflow friction often associated with error mitigation and suppression methods,” Quantum Elements wrote at the time , adding that Orbit lets organizations use “advanced error suppression techniques without requiring deep specialization, while improving circuit execution, and avoiding added processing overhead and extended compiling time.”

More recently, Orbit played a central role in research that could impact both the march to fault-tolerant quantum computers and enabling greater flexibility in designing these systems. In a paper published this month in Nature , researchers with Quantum Elements and the University of Southern California showed that the surface code – a topological quantum error-correction code laid out in a two-dimensional grid and considered among the more practical avenues to large-scale, fault-tolerant systems – can scale error correction even when used with a quantum processing unit (QPU) that doesn’t share a similar grid.

According to Quantum Element executives, running hybrid code on QPUs for error gives engineers breathing room in how they design the computers. It means that there are more options they can look at rather than being hemmed in their designs by having to match a chip’s physical layout with the code. Quantum Elements’ Medalsy said in a statement that the research “shows the power of hybrid approaches to move us towards fault tolerant quantum computing.”

The research used the surface code with the heavy-hex architecture of IBM’s Heron quantum processor, which was first released in 2023 and comes in 133-qubit and 156-qubit (below) configurations. It is used in IBM System 2 and upgraded System One quantum systems.

The heavy-hex architecture is a qubit layout on a hexagonal – honeycomb-like – lattice, which among other features prevents crowded connections to reduce collisions between neighboring qubits. Like this:

“Implementing the surface code on other QPUs with different fixed connectivities is a problem of both fundamental interest and practical importance,” the researchers wrote in their paper. “In light of applications, QPU design may be driven by considerations other than optimal surface code performance, for example to avoid frequency crowding affecting crosstalk and gate performance and to reduce the density of circuit elements, easing thermal management in lithographic fabrication.”

A key challenge was overcoming the reduced connectivity between the two architectures that could lead to delays in the state transfer between non-neighboring qubits and the exposure to noise – which was cause qubits to break up and lost their quantum natures – during such “idle times” meant that the number of errors could grow as the code expands.

Mapping the surface code onto IBM’s architecture also required more routing, another challenge.

The researchers made a number of decisions to make this apparent mismatch work. One of using a depth-efficient error correction code. Surface code, like other error-correction codes, can involve lengthy chains of sequential gates or measurements that introduce the idle time that result in noise that can lead to errors. Depth-efficient codes reduce the number of sequential layers.

They also used the dynamical decoupling – which protects qubits from noise – in Quantum Elements’ Orbit Qiskit function with SWAP-based embedding on the Heron QPU to map logical qubits onto physical hardware. SWAP-based embedding uses SWAP gates, which exchange the quantum states of two qubits.

This led to directional subthreshold scaling, a key step in error correction. It increases the size of the code in a particular direction and reducing a corresponding type of error.

Successfully using the surface code with IBM’s heavy-hex architecture is something Big Blue suggested five years when, when it first announced that heavy-hex would be the foundational topology for all of its quantum devices. IBM researchers laid out their reasoning behind adopting the architecture in a lengthy report that also touched on surface code as an example of the work at the time being done to develop error-correction codes.

“The connectivity of other lattices, such as the square lattice, can be simulated on the heavy-hex lattice with constant overhead by introducing swap operations within a suitably chosen unit cell,” they wrote. “The vertices of the desired virtual lattice can be associated to subsets of vertices in the heavy-hex lattice such that nearest-neighbor gates in the virtual lattice can be simulated with additional two-qubit gates. The connectivity of the heavy-hex lattice can be mapped onto other canonical lattices such as the square lattice with constant cost overhead; it is negligible compared to encoding costs.”

item.title: Vector Search Is Now A Data Type, But The Money Math Has Not Gone Away
item.description:
For a few years it looked like every AI stack would carry a dedicated vector database next to its primary store (for the few who needed it). That moment has passed. Approximate nearest-neighbor search is now everywhere, and is more often than not a column type in the databases that teams already run – Postgres, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, ClickHouse, MongoDB, Redis – and the “do I need a new database for this” question mostly answers itself: No, you don’t.

What did not collapse is the cost math. Vector search as a data type means storing dense embeddings in an existing engine and querying them with approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes alongside the normal filters, joins, and lexical scoring that engine already does, instead of standing up a separate system. That removes an operational surface. It does not remove the physics. At scale, your bill is set by how many bytes each vector occupies in memory, how aggressively you compress them, and where you let them fall out of RAM – and almost none of that depends on which vendor’s logo is on the box.

The Category Collapsed Into The Engines You Already Run

The dedicated vector database was a real category with real engineering behind it. Pinecone launched its managed service in 2021 and effectively named the segment; Milvus, Weaviate, and Qdrant arrived around the same window. The pitch was sound for its time: general-purpose databases had no good ANN index, so semantic search needed a purpose-built home.

The incumbents closed that gap fast. Elasticsearch shipped approximate k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) over the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph algorithm, building on Lucene’s HNSW implementation. OpenSearch has carried a k-NN plugin since its 1.0 release. And pgvector added HNSW in 0.5.0 (August 2023), turning a stock Postgres instance into a credible vector store. MongoDB Atlas Vector Search reached general availability in December 2023. Redis exposed vector similarity in RediSearch 2.4 back in 2022. ClickHouse made its HNSW vector similarity index generally available in 25.8. The same algorithm – HNSW – shows up everywhere, because it is the one that delivers 95+ percent recall without a rebuild step.

The reason this consolidation stuck is not feature parity on paper. It is that production retrieval is rarely pure vector lookup. Useful systems combine lexical scoring, structured filters (tenant, language, ACL, freshness), and aggregations with dense retrieval, then often rerank the merged set. All of that wants to live next to the vectors. A separate vector database forces dual writes, a second consistency model, and a second thing to page someone about at 3 AM. When the engine you already operate can hold the embedding as one more field, the standalone system has to justify itself on more than recall – and usually can’t.

What Actually Drives Cost: Memory Is The Whole Story

HNSW is a graph that has to be traversed with pointer chasing, and that traversal is only fast when the graph and its vectors sit in RAM. The moment nodes spill to disk, latency is dominated by page faults rather than distance computation. So the dominant cost of vector search at scale is memory, and memory scales with the product of vector count and dimensionality.

The per-vector memory footprint for an in-memory HNSW index is well defined. OpenSearch documents it as bytes per vector: the term is the float32 vector itself, is the graph’s per-node connection overhead, and the is roughly 10 percent slack. The consequence is that dimensionality, not document count alone, sets your hardware tier.

The raw numbers are blunt. One million 1,536-dimension float32 vectors – the output size of OpenAI’s – take about 6.1 GB before graph overhead. Ten million of them need roughly 60 GB just for the vectors , all of it RAM-resident for predictable latency. That is the figure that turns a vector feature into a capacity-planning problem.

Graph structure compounds it. HNSW stores neighbor lists at every layer, so the index can run 2-5× the size of the raw vectors , where IVFFlat’s flat per-cell storage stays near 1.1×. This is why the instinctive response to slow vector search - more shards, higher recall settings, bigger – so often makes things worse. Each lever adds memory pressure, fan-out, or per-query CPU, and at scale the slowest shard sets your p99. The recall-versus-throughput curve is steep and non-linear: On standard ANN benchmarks, pushing HNSW from 95 percent to 100 percent recall can cost roughly 7× in throughput . Spending the last two points of recall is usually the most expensive thing in the whole pipeline, and rarely the thing users notice.

The Levers That Bend The Curve: Quantization And Tiering

If memory is the cost, we can definitely use compression to reduce it. Quantization shrinks each vector’s footprint by trading a controllable amount of precision for a large reduction in bytes, usually paired with a rescoring step that re-ranks the top candidates using full-precision vectors held on cheaper storage. This is where real cost reduction happens, and it is mostly orthogonal to vendor choice.

The techniques stack up by aggressiveness:

The numbers behind these are concrete. Lucene’s int8 scalar quantization cuts memory by about 75 percent and keeps raw vectors on disk for rescoring. Binary quantization, which collapses each dimension to a single bit, reaches 32× and works well on high-dimensional embeddings with oversampling - Qdrant reports 0.98 recall@100 on 1536-dim OpenAI embeddings with 4× oversampling. Elasticsearch’s Better Binary Quantization takes a 138M × 1024-dim dataset from roughly 535 GB to about 19 GB .

The other lever is admitting that not all vectors deserve RAM. Disk-based ANN keeps the bulk of the index on SSD with only a compressed copy in memory: Microsoft’s DiskANN indexes a billion points on a single 64 GB machine plus SSD at 95+ percent recall, serving thousands of queries per second. Object-storage tiers push this further - Amazon’s S3 Vectors targets up to 90% lower cost on large vector datasets by trading latency for price. The trade is real and measurable: OpenSearch’s disk-based mode showed p90 latency of 96 ms versus 24 ms for the in-memory path. For agentic retrieval inside a multi-second reasoning loop that is invisible; for interactive autocomplete it is disqualifying. The design move at billion scale vector search is tiering - hot vectors in RAM-backed HNSW, cold vectors quantized on disk or in object storage, whereas some solutions like AWS S3 Vectors and Turbopuffer still allow to enjoy both worlds – large scale vector search at decent performance and low cost.

Where The Self-Managed Versus Managed Line Really Falls

Because the engines have converged on the same algorithm and the same compression toolkit, the self-managed versus managed decision is no longer about capability. Both can do HNSW, both can quantize, both can tier. The line falls on who owns three things: the memory-sizing math, the rescoring and latency cliff, and the routing between hot and cold tiers.

Managed services earn their keep by absorbing the provisioning problem. They size the RAM, isolate vector traffic onto dedicated nodes so it does not contend with operational queries – MongoDB shipped dedicated Search Nodes alongside its Vector Search GA for exactly this reason – and hide the cold-tier fetch behind a single API. You give up access to some of the knobs and you pay a margin, but you stop owning the failure modes.

Self-managed gives you every knob and the bill that comes with using them wrong. You set , , and ef ; you choose the quantization scheme and the oversampling ratio; you decide the rebuild cadence. You also inherit the sharp edges: cold queries against an on-disk HNSW index that page-fault on every traversal step, recall that drifts as data distribution changes, and the fan-out math that makes over-sharding a tail-latency trap.

The decision driver is rarely the technology. It is two questions. Does the vector data already live in an operational store you run – in which case adding a column avoids a whole second system – and what is your latency SLO against your cost ceiling? A team with a strict sub-20 millisecond interactive budget and a small ops crew is usually better served by a managed hot tier. A team that already runs Postgres or OpenSearch at scale, has the headcount to own capacity planning, and wants to control the quantization-and-tiering curve directly will get more out of self-managing it. Pick the engine for the workload, not the other way around.

Here are the key takeaways:

·         The standalone vector database category has largely dissolved. ANN is now a native data type in Postgres (pgvector), the Lucene engines, ClickHouse, MongoDB, and Redis, because production retrieval needs vectors co-located with lexical scoring and filters.

·         Memory is the dominant cost. An in-memory HNSW index needs about 1.1 × (4 × dimension + 8 × M) bytes per vector, and 10M 1536-dim vectors run roughly 60 GB before graph overhead.

·         The recall-versus-throughput curve is non-linear. Chasing the last few points of recall can cost multiples in throughput; “turn the knobs up” usually backfires.·         Quantization and tiering are the levers that move cost, and they are mostly vendor-independent: int8 (4×), Matryoshka truncation (3-12×), binary quantization (32×), and disk/object-storage tiers (up to ~90% cheaper, at a latency cost).

·         Self-managed versus managed is about ownership, not capability. Managed absorbs the sizing math and isolation; self-managed gives you every knob and every failure mode. Decide based on whether the data already lives in your store and on your latency budget versus cost ceiling.

item.title: Accelerated Server Sales Are Themselves Accelerating
item.description:
Do you know what the difference is between an F-18A taking off from the deck of an aircraft carrier to attack long range bombers at 50,000 feet and the revenue trend in the server market?

Me neither.

Either way, you get a stiff neck craning to see the heights.

In the second quarter ended in June, IDC reckons that the world consumed $166.32 billion in servers, an increase of 52 percent year on year and up an amazing 35.6 percent sequentially. We have never seen anything like this before in six decade history of corporate computing. And here is chart showing quarterly sales of servers worldwide from the peak of the Dot Com boom until today to prove it.

We live in a world where half of the revenue being spent on systems are for what we would normally call supercomputers, and two-thirds of the other half is being spent to be the butler and secretary for those supercomputers, with the remaining one-third of that other half being spent for traditional data processing, data analytics, and web infrastructure workloads that use to represent the state of the art in corporate computing only a decade ago.

Of that $162.32 billion spent on server nodes and rackscale systems in Q2 2026, some 52.5 percent of these machines were for GPU-accelerated systems, which works out to $87.4 billion. IDC said in its public quarterly server market tracker report that the average selling price of a GPU-accelerated machine was $170,220, up 43.5 percent year on year from $118,600.

This number can be used to calculate a few insights.

First, we can calculate the number of units sold from this, and it turns out that unit sales of GPU systems were down because of the shift from server nodes that fit many to a rack and have distinct and separate memory domains to rackscale systems where the memory domain stretches across all of the GPUs and usually the CPUs in the rack. In Q2 the shipments of distinct GPU systems fell by 10.7 percent to 513,453 unit, down from 575,278 units in Q2 2025.

What this also tells you is that there are still many, many customers who are buying GPU-accelerated machines with only four or eight GPUs in a fat server node and that all of the buying, despite the talk, is not for rackscale systems with memory coherence across all machines in the rack. You can know this because a Grace-Blackwell NVL72 rackscale system probably costs somewhere around $4 million or so with Nvidia B200 GPUs, and the inference-tuned NVL72 using B300 GPUs costs $5 million or so, give or take a million dollars depending on who you ask.

That ASP for GPU systems given by IDC implies a very large number of low-end systems using cheaper PCI-Express cards, like Nvidia’s RTX Pro 6000. A four-way node using this class of GPU costs on the order of $90,000 to $125,000, depending on the CPU, storage, and network configurations. An eight-way version doubles that to somewhere between $180,000 to $250,000 – which is higher than the ASP. If you want to use B200 or B300 GPUs in an eight-way server node, you are talking maybe $400,000 to $500,000.

This is an inescapable conclusion, unless IDC is doing something really dumb like counting trays in a rackscale system as a node. I do not think this is the case.

Here is the other neat thing that IDC said is that sales of XPU systems – those using other kinds of matrix math engines to run AI workloads and only AI workloads, not general purpose stuff that GPUs can also do – rose by a factor of 3.4X to $27.5 billion in the second quarter. We do not have ASPs from IDC and therefore cannot compute shipments of these devices accurately, but if you assume XPUs cost less than half of a GPU, that puts XPU systems at an ASP of around $85,000 and shipments in Q2 2026 at around 325,000. The shipment numbers here will only grow overt time as all of the clouds and all of the hyperscalers and one of the AI model builders are all working on inference chips. . . . By the way, using these numbers and fiddling up some Q2 2025 XPU ASPs, I think XPU ASPs are up around 45 percent and shipments are up 2.4X. Some of that price increase is due to increasing component costs – as is the case with GPUs, too – and some of it is for more advanced functions on more advanced chip processes.

If you add it all up, you get an average GPU/XPU system costing around $140,000 and around 840,000 units shipped in the second quarter of this year, for a total of $137.35 billion. That gives accelerated machines a 16.1 percent share of units but at 69.1 percent share of revenues.

Plain vanilla servers that do not have acceleration augmentation excepting the vector and (rarely) matrix engines inside of their CPUs accounted for $51.42 billion in sales, IDC says, up 55.8 precent because of the general server refresh cycle and also due to the rise of AI sandbox systems that execute the code and processes created by GenAI inference models. There were just north of 4 million such servers sold in the second quarter, up 16.7 percent. The whole market represented 5.16 million machines, by our math and estimation.

The original design manufacturers are making money hand over first in this exploding market, hauling in $89.66 billion in the June quarter, up 35.2 percent as a group and representing 53.9 percent of all server sales worldwide.

Here is the breakdown by vendor:

Dell has clearly started benefitting from the GenAI boom, as we recently talked about tearing apart its most recent financial results . Dell has blown by Hewlett Packard Enterprise in servers, and has maintained its position as being twice as large as Supermicro. Lenovo had a very good quarter in terms of server revenues, doubling its business year on year. IEIT Systems, which is an arm of Chinese server maker Inspur, actually shrunk, which is odd.

I strongly suspect profits as a share of revenue are down for all of these server makers as they eat the GenAI bear meat with too little fat. The difference is that with servers, you can make it up in volume, and with lean bear meat, eating more and more to sate your hunger will kill you.

Nvidia can sure get rich selling everybody compute engines and networking for GenAI, though.

item.title: The GenAI Boom Accelerates And Transforms Ethernet Switching
item.description:
The server market is exploding thanks to the GenAI boom, and the Ethernet switch and router markets are finally starting to respond in sympathy with good growth. But don’t get too excited. It probably won’t be able to grow as fast as it might because of component shortages, but then again, demand outstripping supply and creating its own kind of rise thanks to price increases.

It is a good time to be pricing out any kind of semiconductor. You can just get a red grease pencil and scratch out an old price and write down a newer high price because you feel like it. What is anyone gonna do about it?

In the second quarter, which is the latest one for which IDC has market data compiled, switch revenues rose by 43.4 percent to $18.91 billion, which was also a 23.1 percent growth sequentially from switch sales Q1 2026.

The router market, which has been under pressure for more than a decade as more and more routing functions are added to Ethernet switch ASICs, also managed to grow very nicely, up 22.8 percent to $4.51 billion in the period and up 20.1 percent sequentially. Yes, companies such as service providers, telcos, neoclouds, and others that cannot write their own routing software for Ethernet switches – as they hyperscalers and cloud builders do – still buy routers. We don’t spend a lot of time looking at the routers from Cisco Systems, Juniper Networks, Huawei Technology, Nokia, Ericsson, and a few others, but their routing gear is still important for a lot of enterprises. It is not at the heart of the system even if it is what links the datacenter to the outside world at a lot of companies.

Let’s take a look at Ethernet switching in general, and then drill down into the datacenter portion of the market that The Next Platform cares about.

Her’s the overall revenue chart by vendor supplied by IDC:

This is an interesting chart of sales by vendor, but it is very hard to see the trend lines for each vendor, and it does not provide more than five quarters of data so you can’t really get a feel for just how much more money is being spent on Ethernet switchery compared to the past.

So let’s be clear: This is record sales for Ethernet switches, and it is not only because of GenAI systems in the datacenters, but because edge and campus networks have to be upgraded to feed into GenAI systems.

The public IDC dataset for the Ethernet switch market only goes back to the third quarter of 2013, so we cannot see what happened before, during, and after the Dot Com boom, the Dot Com bust, or the Great Recession, three of the big economic events that changed buying patterns. We can see the effect of the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 through 2022, and we are seeing the effect of the GenAI boom.

Here is a much better Ethernet switch chart by vendors, so you can see who is rising and who is falling:

And here is the table that runs from 2024 through Q2 2026 that gives you the numbers behind portions of those lines shown above:

Cisco’s overall Ethernet revenues grew by 36.2 percent to $5.43 billion in Q2 2026, but Nvidia grew by 2.8X thanks to its enormous GenAI systems business and its attachment rate for its Spectrum-X switches for scaling out its DGX server nodes and its NVL72 rackscale systems.

Nvidia’s $3.86 billion dwarfed Cisco nemesis Arista Networks, which grew 37.6 percent to $2.53 billion. Even after eating Juniper Networks, the Ethernet switch business of Hewlett Packard Enterprise only grew by 6.1 percent to $1.15 billion. Still, that is a lot of incremental business for HPE, whose Ethernet business was largely wireless stuff under the Aruba brand. Huawei Technology has been jockeying with HPE for the past several years, and this quarter it came out ahead with $1.55 billion in revenues, up 28.6. IDC is no longer providing figures for the collective original design manufacturers (ODMs), but I estimate they raked in $3.56 billion, up 2.43X year on year. The other vendors in the market have seen their market share tank, provided my ODM number is correct.

Of course, we are less interested in campus and edge networking than what goes on inside the datacenter, and luckily, IDC provides a split between these two categories:

To be fair, IDC used to give out revenues and port counts for datacenter and campus/edge Ethernet switch sales, and stopped talking about ports after Q2 2022. I have been doing my best to fill in the gap since then.

In Q2, datacenter Ethernet switch revenues totaled $12.3 billion, up 64.5 percent year on year and up 23 percent sequentially. I reckon that around 129.5 million ports were sold into the datacenter market for scale up, scale out, and scale across networks – and mostly for scale out. (This will change.) The datacenter comprised 65.1 percent of revenues and 42.8 percent of ports shipped, in my augmentation of IDC’s data.

When you drill down into the switch port speeds, anything above 200 Gb/sec is very likely for datacenter use cases, while 100 Gb/sec and 10 Gb/sec networks are split between datacenter and campus/edge use cases.

In the quarter, sales of switches with 800 Gb/sec ports were exclusively sold for datacenter use cases, and revenues rose by 6.1X year on year to $5.07 billion, which was a 41.5 sequential increase. IDC gave us a hint that in the datacenter sector that 35.9 percent of ports shipping in Q1 2026 were from 800 Gb/sec switches, and in Q2 2026, this rose to 41.2 percent of all datacenter switch ports. There is a huge wave of adoption for 800 Gb/sec in GenAI clusters, and interestingly, the cost per port is coming here as the hyperscalers and cloud builders negotiate hard for discounts and vendors make the revenue up in volume even as there are shortages of components. I reckon there were 35.3 million 800 Gb/sec ports sold in Q1 2026 and 54.3 million sold in Q2 2026.

Sales of Ethernet switches with 200 Gb/sec or 400 Gb/sec ports, which are pretty much only sold for datacenter use cases, rose by 71.6 percent to $6.35 billion. I reckon that 35.8 million ports running at these speeds were sold in Q2.

The prices per port for 800 Gb/sec or 200/400 Gb/sec switches came down a little bit in my model, but not by much. The number of ports on machines is growing as machines with 51.2 Tb/sec and 102.4 Tb/sec ASICs are coming to market, and that is driving up switch revenues as customer hunt for higher radix, higher bandwidth, or both in their switches. And it won’t be long before 1.6 Tb/sec switches are ramping in volume for high-end GenAI systems and low latency Ethernet with UALink or ESUN protocols becomes an alternative to Nvidia’s NVLink/NVSwitch combo.

Let’s drill down into the datacenter part of the overall Ethernet market now. This is where most of the action is. Here is a plot showing the top three vendors plus the ODM collective:

And here is a table that shows the data since Q1 2023:

item.title: Bull Beats Out HPE For Next-Gen Lumi AI Supercomputer
item.description:
In many ways, Europe is more traditional than America, and this is particularly so when it comes to GenAI infrastructure. While all of the national supercomputing labs have built systems that can do both traditional HPC simulation and modeling, in Europe AI efforts to custom tune GenAI and traditional machine learning models are focused on the national labs, not in AI model builders.

Of course, that is because the major AI model builders are based on the United States and China. But no matter. Our point is that with the national labs leading both HPC and GenAI efforts across Europe, there are grownups in the room who are applying GenAI to scientific challenges funded by governments while also providing compute allocations to businesses in Europe that are trying to build AI models as well as use HPC tools to design products.

The national labs are not financed by private equity or the makers of GPU accelerators or the big clouds, so they have to make do with less – two or three orders of magnitude less money and less compute. But that’s fine. They are still getting more compute capacity than they ever had access to, and they can go to sleep at night knowing that they are unequivocally trying to do good in the world.

So it is with the upcoming next generation Lumi-AI supercomputer – which will be one component in what is being called the Lumi AI factory to borrow a term coined by Nvidia – that is being funded by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking and that will be installed at the Center for Scientific Computation (CSC) facilities in Kajaani, Finland. (Lumi is Finnish for “snow on the ground,” but the mascot of the machine is a white wolf. They could have named the machine “susi,” which is wolf in Finnish. . . .)

The original Lumi hybrid supercomputer cluster, a mix of CPU-only, CPU-GPU, big memory CPU, object storage, Lustre parallel file system storage, and flash storage nodes, was first unveiled way back in October 2020 . That hybrid machine was expected to have a total of 552 petaflops of aggregate computing at FP64 precision. The Lumi-C partition, with over 200,000 CPUs cores based on AMD Epyc processors would have about 2 petaflops of FP64 compute, with the Lumi-G partition based on AMD Instinct processors having about 550 petaflops of double precision floating point processing. The Lumi cluster of clusters would also have 30 PB of Ceph object storage, 80 PB of Lustre storage, and 7 PB of flash storage. The nodes within each partition as well as linking those partitions together was based on the “Rosetta” 200 Gb/sec Slingshot-10 interconnect, with Hewlett Packard Enterprise as the main contractor for the system.

The whole shebang was given a $237 million budget by EuroHPC, which worked out to about $431 per teraflops. The Lumi-C partition was delivered in the summer of 2021, and the Lumi-G GPU partition was delivered at the end of 2021. These partitions were operational in June 2022. The Lumi-G partition was ranked as the number 11 supercomputer in the Top500 rankings in June of this year, so it is no slouch even though it was four years old at the time.

The Lumi-C partition has 1,536 nodes, each of which are equipped with a pair of 64-core “Milan” Epyc 7763 processors spinning at 2.45 GHz. That comes to a total of 196,860 cores, to be precise. This partition is ranked number 262 on the June Top500 rankings, with a peak theoretical performance of 7.29 petaflops and a sustained Linpack performance of 6.3 petaflops, which is a very respectable 82.6 percent computational efficiency in a 1.22 megawatt power envelope. That works out to 5.18 gigaflops per watt.

This machine uses a 200 Gb/sec Slingshot 11 interconnect to lash the nodes together.

The Lumi-G partition has 2,978 nodes, with each one having a single 64-core “Trento” Epyc 7A53 custom processor with four “Aldebaran” MI250X GPU accelerators hanging off that. (The Trento chip was custom built for the “Frontier” supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the US, and provided memory coherence across AMD CPUs and GPUs before that was officially commercially available.) That is a total of 2,978 Trento CPUs, with 190,592 cores, and 11,912 Aldebaran GPUs, with a total of 2.62 million compute units and 167.7 million streaming processors. The nodes in the Lumi-G partition are linked by a 200 Gb/sec Slingshot-11 interconnect. This partition of the Lumi machine has a peak theoretical performance of 531.5 petaflops at FP64 precision, and rated 379.7 petaflops on the Linpack test, which is a computational efficiency of 71.4 percent. This partition weighs in at 7.1 megawatts and delivers 53.43 gigaflops per watt on Linpack, which is more than 10X better power efficiency than the CPU-only partition.

What I know about the future Lumi-AI partition, which is really an upgrade to the Lumi-G partition that I assume will stay in production given the value of those AMD GPUs and the scarcity of GPU capacity on the world, is that it will offer 10X the performance on AI workloads and “around 2X” the performance on FP64 HPC workloads.

It will not be hard to beat the AI performance of the MI250X, which supported INT4 and INT8 data formats as well as FP16 formats, but the performance was the same for all three. So INT4 and INT8 were not precisely native on the Aldebaran GPUs, but grafted on top of FP16, which was fine for that time. But with the Altair GPUs that are being packaged as the MI430X aimed at both HPC and AI workloads (unlike the top-end Altair MI455X, which is aimed at AI inference and training), FP4 and FP8 processing is native, so you get a multiplicative effect as you trim down from FP16. So 4X of that 10X is coming from the shift from FP16 down to FP4. So that leaves 2.5X more raw performance at FP16 comparing the Altair GPU used in the MI430X to the Aldebaran GPU used in the MI250X.

This means, of course, that the node count in the Lumi-AI partition should be a lot smaller, even if the devices themselves will certainly burn more electricity and therefore generate more heat.

Let’s figure out that node count on Lumi-AI.

The MI250X is rated at 47.9 teraflops on its vector units and 95.7 teraflops on its matrix units. The MI430X has a peak of 288 teraflops on FP64 workloads, and AMD was not precise about this being on vector or matrix units. It doesn’t have to be because the MI430X delivers 288 teraflops on both vector and matrix units. If you do the math on the Lumi-G partition, it looks like CSC Finland was counting the vector FP64 performance (47.9 teraflops times four GPUs per node times 2,978 nodes is a peak of 570.6 petaflops. (We don’t know why this doesn’t match the 531.5 Rpeak on the Linpack test.)

If you want 2X performance on the GPUs at FP64 vector for Lumi-AI, then you only need 3,962 MI430X GPUs, and that works out to a mere 991 nodes, a 66.7 percent reduction in node count for the AI partition. (This breaks the exascale barrier, with 1.14 exaflops peak, which is psychologically important. Each node will, however, burn about 2X the energy, at 5 kilowatts for the Venice-Altair 1x4 board compared to 2.5 kilowatts for the Trento-Aldebaran 1x4 board. And that means the Lumi-AI partition will probably consume about 5 megawatts, assuming 991 nodes, which is a 33 percent reduction compared to the Lumi-G partition.

The weird thing is that when we do the math on this number of nodes to derive the AI performance at FP64, we only get an 8X performance increase. You need 1,240 nodes with four MI430X GPUs in Lumi-AI to get a 10X increase over Lumi-G at 4-bit precision. That might mean that CSC Finland will get an extra 25 percent more FP64 vector performance than it is talking about.

I’m going with 1,240 nodes with 4,960 MI430X GPUs for my guess, which is a 58.4 percent reduction in GPU partition node count and about 6.2 megawatts of system power for Lumi-AI. Both Bull, the primary contractor for the Lumi-AI partition, and CSC Finland were clear that AI performance would be 10X higher and HPC performance would be “about 2X.” Why HPC centers are imprecise in their statements is a mystery, and it is counterintuitive for an organization that lives by precision. Go figure.

Using a 256-core “Venice” Epyc 9006 processor, the Lumi-AI partition will have 317,440 cores, which is an appreciable number of compute units to help orchestrate those GPUs and which is 66.7 percent higher than the core count in the current Lumi-G partition.

Given all of this, and a price tag of €387.8 million for the Lumi-AI partition, converting that to US dollars yields a cost of $445.1 million and against a peak FP64 performance of 1.43 exaflops for the Lumi-AI partition, you get a $312 per teraflops at peak. This is a 27.6 percent lower cost per teraflops than the $431 per teraflops peak that the entire Lumi cluster cost when it was installed in 2021. It is not known if the Lumi CPU-only partition and the various storage clusters will also be upgraded under the Lumi-AI contract, but we presume this to be the case. Which makes this an apples-to-apples overall system comparison.

That CSC Finland and its EuroHPC funding arm went with Bull over HPE in this deal is not a big surprise, really. EuroHPC wants to buy European as much as possible. Moreover, while Slingshot is an Ethernet variant that can be possibly modified to adhere to Ultra Ethernet Consortium hardware, Bulls BXI protocol is being adapted to run on UEC hardware and make use of its various features. Which means Bull customers using the BullSequana XH3500 systems will have a choice of switchery when they want to do scale out clustering.

The Lumi-AI GPU partition is expected to be installed in the second half of 2027 in a new datacenter located in Kajaani. Finland, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Norway, and Poland are kicking in money alongside the European Union’s EuroHPC JU. The precise amounts everyone is paying was not disclosed.

The Lumi AI factory will not only include this new AMD Venice-Altair cluster, but will also have a quantum computing element dubbed Lumi-IQ. The quantum system is being built by IQM Quantum Computers, a Finnish company that has raised €600 million in venture capital so far and that has aspirations to be Europe’s top quantum computing supplier. The company is preparing to go public and has a valuation of $1.8 billion at this time.

The plan is to installed a Halocene H4 system at CSC Finland in 2027, which will have 150 physical cubits and support 5 logical qubits. Upgrades will be done in 2028 to improve error correction and to improve the reliability of logical qubits. In 2029, CSC Finland will get an upgrade to a Halocene H5 quantum computer, which will have an unknown number of physical qubits but will deliver at least 9 logical qubits. That should imply 270 physical qubits to deliver those local qubits.

item.title: Infleqtion And Nvidia Reduce Physical-to-Logical Qubit Ratio in Quantum Computers
item.description:
A lot of advancements are being made in quantum computing that move beyond the basics of quantum processors (QPUs) and hardware fundamentals. Companies are expanding out into the architectural realm , subsystems for these machines are being pulled together, and quantum software and algorithms are being developed, while efforts to make quantum computing scalable and integrated into HPC environments are being made.

Still, a key to getting quantum computing from the research phase to commercial viability is solving the error correction challenge. Qubits are notoriously fragile and can split apart – and lose their quantum properties – due to various “noises” like light, sound, temperature, or the activity of other qubits, and a quantum system that makes too many errors isn’t commercially viable. To improve error correction, multiple entangled physical qubits are grouped together to create logical qubits.

However, that comes at a price, from the technical challenges of needing thousands of physical qubits to make a single logical one to cooling and manufacturing costs to adding more noise. Given that, reducing the number of physical qubits per logical qubit is important.

“An unofficial law of physics is ‘there’s no such thing as a free lunch,’” Quantinuum executives wrote earlier this year . “Creating high quality, low error-rate logical qubits often costs many physical qubits, thus reducing the size of calculations you can run, despite your new, lower-than-ever error rates.”

Work is being done researchers and standards groups to reduce the logical-to-physical qubit ratio. Vendors also are making gains. Sheir Yarkoni, director of quantum software for Qarakal Quantum, told The Next Platform that the startup’s new Pangaea architecture will reduce the physical qubit requirements by 10 times. D-Wave has said the same about its developing dual-rail superconducting systems, and Quantinuum in a paper published in March detailed its technology that creates 48 error-corrected and 64 error-detected logical qubits out of 98 physical qubits.

At the IEEE Quantum Week event this week in Toronto, Infleqtion executives said that, thanks to the integration of their open source quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) software library and Nvidia’s new CUDA-Q Logical – a logical orchestration and compiler layer also unveiled at the show – they built a validated high-rate quantum error correction code that uses 98 physical data qubits for 18 logical qubits, or about 5.4 physical qubits per logical qubit and driving an 18.4 percent encoding rate.

Infleqtion, which uses neutral atoms in its Sqale systems (below) to create its qubits, used an early-access version of Nvidia’s CUDA-Q Logical software to build a hypergraph-product simplex (HGPS) code block, create stabilizers and logical operators, and put in place the necessary underlying algebra, Victory Omole, senior quantum research engineer for the vendor, wrote in a report. The code also contains 49 X checks and 49 Z checks, used to detect specific types of physical errors and each of weight six.

The canonical logical representatives returned by qLDPC software have weight four.

“Many familiar QEC constructions devote a large number of data qubits to each logical qubit,” Omole wrote. “High-rate qLDPC codes change that arithmetic by encoding multiple logical qubits in one block while keeping each stabilizer check sparse. The appeal is obvious: if the rest of the architecture cooperates, more of the machine can carry useful logical information.”

Doing the work in that sentence is “if the rest of the architecture cooperates.” As Omele wrote, while such numbers as the physical-to-logical qubit ratio are good, other factors in a quantum computing architecture – syndrome ancilla qubits (used to perform error syndrome measurements), scheduling, readout, control, and classical decoding, among others – need to ensure those numbers are preserved throughout the system stack.

That’s where CUDA-Q Logical comes in. Infleqtion’s gLDPC software provides the underlying mathematics for the code.

“CUDA-Q Logical supplies the logical ownership, block allocation, and compilation model,” he wrote. “The code interface in CUDA-Q Logical takes sparse row supports. A small adapter converts the dense NumPy arrays, after which the qLDPC software-generated checks and logical operators can be declared as an 18-port CUDA-Q Logical code.”

Using gLDPC and CUDA-Q Logical together, Infleqtion engineers were able to build the code and validate the structure, which then lead to the creation of the compiler pipeline. The block coming out of the pipeline is confirmed to hold multiple logical qubits inside a single encoded structure, the engineers wrote, adding that the pipeline builds on the architecture research done by Fred Chong, Infleqtion’s chief scientist for quantum software.

The integration of Infleqtion’s and Nvidia’s technologies not only led to the narrowed physical-to-logical qubit ratio, but also that the stabilizer’s matrices and the X and Z checks commute, and that the CUDA-Q code has 18 logical ports and 49 each X and Z checks. In addition, the workflow that was compiled ensure two distinct logical qubit owners within a single encoded block.

“This integration focuses on code construction, logical ownership, and compilation,” Omele wrote. “In coming work, we plan to extend this workflow through physical syndrome extraction, neutral-atom noise modeling, detector generation, and decoder benchmarking.”

The work in Chong’s laboratory focuses on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays that are good for high-rate qLDPC codes due to their parallel operations and flexible connectivity.

“For our team, the opportunity is to trace that promise through a real machine model,” he wrote. “That means accounting for where ancillas live, how atoms move, which checks can run in parallel, how leakage and loss appear in readout, and whether the classical decoder can keep up with the syndrome stream. Logical performance emerges from the coordination of hardware, control, compilation, and classical compute.”

Infleqtion was founded in 2007, spinning out from atomics physics research at the University of Colorado initially under the name ColdQuanta before rebranding at Infleqtion in 2022. The company’s plans include an aggressive roadmap that sees it reaching more than 1,000 logical qubits by 2030.

The work with Nvidia and its CUDA-Q Logical software is only the latest step in what has been a busy year for the company. Recent events include a $20 million follow-on contract with NASA to continue developing the Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder, a Jet Propulsion Laboratory mission to fly the first space-based quantum gravity sensor, the opening of the Colorado Quantum Innovation Center, and the awarding of three projects in the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission , which aims to accelerate research and innovation using AI and includes a quantum arm with the goal of deploying the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer.

Infleqtion executives last week also announced plans to bring together the company’s neutral-atom quantum systems and sensors with Cisco Systems’ quantum networking portfolio in a joint R&D effort to scale quantum computing by networking systems together. Cisco last year began laying the groundwork for a quantum network architecture , and in April unveiled its Universal Quantum Switch , a working prototype for connecting quantum systems from different vendors that use different modalities and quantum sensors to create a single network.

Infleqtion engineers noted that neutral atoms work naturally with photons, which are particles of light used to carry quantum information across networks, making their systems well suited for connecting into such networks and to work with within Cisco’s vision of a modality-agnostic network architecture.

item.title: How To Smash The Memory Wall Plaguing High Performance Systems
item.description:
In my day-to-day work, I process massive data volumes, wrestling with large-scale .parquet files, column-major databases, and algorithms that analyze information through a geometric or matrix lens.

As I run complex analytical queries and execute heavy table shuffles or joins across various platforms, I repeatedly watch today’s most advanced server processors fall short of their peak theoretical performance. A primary culprit? Cores sitting idle, waiting for data transfers from RAM. Our ultra-fast cores remain trapped in a 40-year-old architectural mindset, viewing memory as a rigid, linear, one-dimensional array. Meanwhile, modern software is deliberately engineered to cluster data intelligently by related regions and columns.

When 128 cores concurrently drive modern analytical workloads, this traditional memory model breaks down. Cores relentlessly request narrow 64-byte cache lines scattered haphazardly across the RAM footprint.
